extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporters on how to prepare for, take notes on, and write accurate, newsworthy accounts of public speeches and lectures for newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate condensation with direct quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: To report a speech largely by direct quotes and have a short (e.g., 200-word) story reflect accurately the speaker's much longer address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the most exacting reporter's tasks; anyone can paraphrase, but reproducing the speaker's voice in a compressed form requires skill. Aim to capture the speaker's key phrasing so the short piece mirrors the tone and content of the full 6,500-word speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shorthand, abbreviations, and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a personal shorthand or list of symbols (e.g., 'E' for economics, 'R' for Republicans) to speed note-taking without formal stenography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supersimplified shorthand or a built symbol list can be profitably learned quickly; full mastery of stenography usually isn't worth the weeks of effort. Salvage useful college abbreviations and build new ones suited to your beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take full-sentence notes (subject-verb-object)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equip each note with subject, verb, and object so each jotting has only one meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full-sentence notes prevent double meanings and guessing later. Examples: replace fragment 'Action in 6 mos.' with 'Pension foes will start attack in 6 mos.' Articles and modifiers can be omitted and abbreviations used; the key is to make each note unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fragmentary guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on splintery, fragmentary jottings that admit multiple interpretations and force the reporter to guess meaning later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragmentary notes lead to divergent, possibly wrong stories. If the speaker can't be reached later, guesswork produces stale copy. Remedy: take clearer notes (full sentences) to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, conscious listening
rubrics_metrics.description: Hear every sentence of the speech; listening is a deliberate, premeditated effort and may require 'hoodwinking' yourself into interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sitting slouched and thinking of other things yields crude, inaccurate notes. The reporter must be far more attentive than the average audience member; even counterfeit interest is acceptable if it produces focused listening and a better story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on memory-reporting (unless seasoned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory reporting (reproducing long passages from sparse jottings) is feasible only for very experienced reporters who have trained memories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasoned reporters who have heard millions of words may reproduce long passages from minimal jottings; inexperienced reporters should not attempt this or they'll risk inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch speaker mannerisms and signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe a speaker's physical and vocal trademarks (gaze, throat-clearing, reading behavior, stance shifts) to anticipate when important lines are coming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ten minutes of attentive watching reveals patterns that signal climactic sentences or topic shifts, allowing the reporter to tighten listening at critical moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand typical speech structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Know that professional speakers usually stage-set at the start, present less significant points during middle attention dips, and reserve strong, staccato doctrines for the close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening to learn the speaker's outline and mannerisms; expect key quotable material either early or at the end. The reporter must master the speech in its entirety to compress it intelligently into a short story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use speakers' pet expressions for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture trademark phrases ('Heaven forfend') and use them in the story to give authenticity and individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note such expressions and create shorthand markers (e.g., 'HF') so you can reproduce them accurately in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test acoustics and choose seat
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first few minutes to test the hall's acoustics and, if necessary, change seat to ensure you can hear the talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hall is unfamiliar, adjust seating early so you won't miss key lines and can take accurate notes throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate where quotes will come from by speaker type
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize differences in speakers: ministers may place points unpredictably; professional touring speakers follow a standardized pattern; scientists often reserve solid, contemporary material for the final part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor listening strategy: ministers may put key points in the middle, scientists often yield quotable material in the last 15 minutes, and greenhorns are unpredictable — be alert throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate technical talks for general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a talk is technical or for a specialist audience, ask the speaker (or audience members) to summarize in nontechnical language and explain importance to general readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the speaker is unresponsive, other audience members may help. Never leave baffled; a few minutes of post-speech questioning can produce usable paragraphs and rescue the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle foreign-language speeches resourcefully
rubrics_metrics.description: For talks in another language, arrive early to find a translator or a bilingual audience member to sit with you; if necessary, rely largely on paraphrase rather than direct quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators may bias shades of meaning; it's safer to paraphrase. If no translator is available, note audience reaction timings and later ask an intelligent listener to summarize high spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify quotations and ask for speaker copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview the speaker immediately after the talk to verify quotations and paraphrases; request carbon copies of the manuscript or abstracts when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verifying quotes is the reporter's chief protection against misquotation complaints. Many professionals bring carbons expressly for reporters and expect you to ask. However, do not let abstracts or advance copies substitute for attendance — they may be toned down or not reflect what was actually said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not skip the lecture because of advance copy
rubrics_metrics.description: An advance copy or mailed manuscript is not an excuse for missing the actual speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers may miss trains, omit or change passages, or deliver differently in person. Relying on an advance copy risks quoting things the audience didn't hear or missing spontaneous, more vivid material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain brisk note-taking throughout the talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Take notes as briskly in the middle 'throat-clearing' portion as at the end; the reporter must master all parts to compress effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the middle may be less likely to yield a lead, failing to note it accurately results in only average-audience comprehension and poor compression into a short story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use post-speech interviewing when stuck
rubrics_metrics.description: If you missed parts, honestly tell the speaker and ask what sections might interest general readers and how to say them in plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few minutes of polite questioning usually produces a usable summary; leaving in a fog without attempting a translation is poor reporting.
